title: The Weight of Glory and the Two Dwellings
english: … saying: “Whoever seeks his own glory is not true, but whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true” (John 7:18).

On 2 Corinthians 4:6: “In the face of Jesus Christ” stands for “through Jesus Christ,” that is, because of him. “For the illumination of the knowledge”: because this knowledge was not discovered by reasoning but laid open by revelation.
The second catena form adds: It was made known by revelation and illumination, for no human being wrapped in a scrap of flesh could ever have reached it.

On 2 Corinthians 4:7–9: By these words and the ones that follow he shows that God does not let us be tested beyond our strength (1 Corinthians 10:13). Persecutors may afflict us, but we are never so hemmed in that we have no escape and no way out anywhere; for God makes room for those afflicted for godliness' sake. That is why David says, “In affliction you made room for me” (Psalm 4:1).
On 2 Corinthians 4:10: We always carry about the dying because we are always in danger for Christ's sake, sharing in the sufferings of Christ.
On 2 Corinthians 4:11: The Lord was handed over to death for us; we are handed over for our own good, because of Jesus, so that we may come to share in his life.
On 2 Corinthians 4:12: Because of the preaching the apostles were in danger, yet they preached so that believers might live; that is what “but life in you” means.

On 2 Corinthians 4:13: For, he says, under the law there is a spirit of slavery, but under grace a spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15). He said that we have the same spirit that David had, and he added “of faith”: the same spirit of faith, not the slavery of the law.
The second catena form adds: We have the same spirit, he says, as David, who spoke by faith when he said, “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Psalm 116:10). This alone is common to the New and the Old.

On 2 Corinthians 4:17–18: If deaths, dangers and trials dogged him, how is the affliction “light”? How is it “momentary”? His trials stayed with him and pursued him into old age. How then is the affliction of the saints light? Or rather, it is plainly light when set against the glory of the age to come and the good things laid up for the righteous; beside these, even the heaviest trials seem light to me. The afflictions are not simply light but light beyond all measure, because they fall far short of the greatness of the glory; a large body is also a heavy one. Or else he spoke of “weight” by a metaphor from the scales: weighed against the afflictions, the glory proves very heavy indeed. By “momentary” he means temporary; for even if what afflicts and grieves us lasts long, it looks brief beside the endlessness of the glory.

On 2 Corinthians 5:1–2: “The house of the tent”: the house, not the tent; for our dwelling here comes to an end, while the tent rises again. By “house” he meant our way of life, both the mortal one and the one we wait for. Next, though, he shows that by “dwelling” he means corruption and incorruption.

The second catena form adds: By “the house of the tent” he means the body. Even if it is destroyed, he says, in trials and dangers for Christ's sake, we will lay it aside as a perishable house and the last of things made by hands, and we will find in heaven another house, which God provides, imperishable and not made by hands. By “to be clothed over” he shows that the perishable flesh rises and puts on immortality over itself; for one is said to be clothed over when a garment goes on top of another. He speaks of two houses, the mortal and the one we wait for, and of two dwellings, corruption and incorruption, because we are released from the one and clothed over with the other. By “the dwelling from heaven” he means the incorruption that comes from heaven, since it is not made by hands but is a gift of God.
